title: When Cache Pressure Becomes a Trap: Metastability in Agent Serving
trick: Count every active agent session's context, tool-idle included, as the prefix-cache working set; past about twice cache capacity, misses lengthen sessions, sessions enlarge the working set, and the engine stays trapped after the surge.
framing_stripped: Called 'metastable failure' with 'population–cache feedback' and a controller named Basin; it is (a) a measured bistability in SGLang prefill-decode (PD) disaggregated serving of replayed coding-agent sessions, where the departure rate of sessions first rises then falls with the number of active sessions because the prefix hit rate collapses once the aggregate context of active sessions passes about $1.9\times$ the cache, so a base load that was healthy before a ten-minute surge is trapped after it (sec. 3, 5), plus (b) a one-dimensional fluid (population) model with a stable and an unstable equilibrium, a memory criterion for which resource (prefix cache or decode KV) limits first (eq. 2), and (c) an operating-systems import: Denning's working-set admission and page-fault-frequency budget adaptation applied to agent sessions, with each session's peak context predicted at its first call, a fixed arrival-plus-size priority on all queues, idle decode memory lent as an extra prefix-cache tier, and shedding when long-run arrivals exceed the profiled peak departure rate (sec. 6).
method_equations: Population balance (eq. 1, sec. 5.1): $N(t)$ is the number of active sessions, tool-executing ones included; $\lambda(t)$ the session arrival rate; $K$ the mean number of model calls per session; $g$ the mean tool gap; $X(N)$ the call throughput at population $N$. $$\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda(t) - \frac{X(N)}{K}.$$ $X(N)$ is a smooth minimum of three bounds: the closed-loop bound $N/(g + L_0)$ with $L_0$ the unloaded call latency; the prefill bound $\mu_p / u(N)$ with $\mu_p$ the saturated prefill throughput in tokens per second and $$u(N) = \max\bigl(n_{\mathrm{new}},\ (1 - h(W/C))\,P\bigr)$$ the uncached tokens per call, where $P$ is the mean prompt length, $n_{\mathrm{new}}$ the new suffix length, $W = N\bar{c}$ the working set ($\bar{c}$ the mean context length over active sessions), $C$ the prefix-cache capacity in tokens and $h(\cdot)$ the measured hit-rate curve of Fig. 6b (plateau about 0.95, falling to about 0.3 at $W/C \approx 2$); and the decode bound, the number of requests whose KV fits in decode memory divided by their decode time. Departure curve $D(N) = X(N)/K$ rises to a peak at $N^{\ast}$ then falls to a low-reuse floor $D_{\mathrm{low}}$; a base rate $\lambda$ with $D_{\mathrm{low}} < \lambda < D(N^{\ast})$ meets the curve at a stable equilibrium $N_s$ and an unstable one $N_u$; a surge pushing $N$ past $N_u$ leaves departures below arrivals permanently (Fig. 9a). Vulnerability condition (eq. 2): the cache cliff sits near $N_c \approx 1.9\,C/\bar{c}$ and decode memory fills near $N_d \approx D_{\mathrm{KV}}/(f\bar{c})$, with $D_{\mathrm{KV}}$ the decode KV capacity in tokens and $f$ the fraction of active sessions currently in service (not in a tool); the cache cliff precedes decode saturation when $$C \lesssim \frac{D_{\mathrm{KV}}}{2f}.$$ Longer tool gaps lower $f$ and more decode instances raise $D_{\mathrm{KV}}$, both favouring cache-first failure. Entry control (eq. 3, sec. 5.3): $Q(t)$ sessions waiting for their first call, $I(t)$ their admission rate, $$\frac{dN}{dt} = I(t) - D(N), \qquad \frac{dQ}{dt} = \lambda(t) - I(t);$$ with resident-first ordering holding $N \approx N^{\ast}$ (eq. 4) $dQ/dt \simeq \lambda(t) - D(N^{\ast})$, so a backlog of $S$ sessions drains in about $S/(D(N^{\ast}) - \lambda)$, and summing gives $d(N+Q)/dt = \lambda - D(N)$: under sustained $\lambda > D(N^{\ast})$ the total backlog grows at least at rate $\lambda - D(N^{\ast})$, so only added departure capacity or shedding of that excess bounds it. Little's law is used for the steady population, mean population $= \lambda T$ with $T$ the mean session lifetime including tool time (sec. 3.4). Basin controller (sec. 6, Table 1, Algorithm 1): $C = \max(C_G, C_H)$ with $C_G$ the aggregate prefill GPU cache and $C_H$ the inclusive host tier; $L$ the lent decode capacity; $C_{\mathrm{eff}} = \max(C, C_G + L)$; cliff $W_c = \kappa x_k C_{\mathrm{eff}}$ with $x_k \approx 1.9$ the reference knee and $\kappa$ a profiled per-deployment scale; reference budget $B_0 = \min(m W_c, C_{\mathrm{eff}})$ with margin $m = 0.9$; adapted budget $B$ raised when sessions are parked and the hit rate stays on its plateau, lowered when reuse deteriorates (page-fault-frequency control). Admission of queue head $i$ when $$\sum_{j \in \mathrm{res}} \hat{W}_j + \hat{W}_i \le B,$$ where $\hat{W}_j$ is session $j$'s predicted peak context (input plus output tokens), fixed at its first call; admission engages at $W \ge B_0$ and releases when $W < \alpha_R B_0$ has held for a cool-down ($\alpha_R = 0.8$); lending engages at $W \ge \alpha_L B_0$ ($\alpha_L = 0.8$), capped at $\phi = 0.5$ of decode memory; ordering engages at $W \ge \alpha_O B_0$ ($\alpha_O = 0.9$) or under a persistent backlog. Fixed priority $$p_i = a_i + \hat{W}_i / r,$$ with $a_i$ the arrival time and $r = 30$ tokens per second converting predicted tokens into seconds (smaller first; a later arrival $j$ with $a_j > a_i + \hat{W}_i/r$ can never pass $i$). Shedding: when the long-run mean arrival rate $\bar{\lambda}$ exceeds the profiled peak departure rate $\lambda_c$ and the highest-priority parked session has waited $T_s = 15$ min, drop the lowest-priority parked session, one per control interval $\Delta = 30$ s (5 s under backlog). Predictor (sec. 6.5): per-workload ridge regression of $\log$ peak context on TF-IDF features of the task text plus the $\log$ lengths of task text and first prompt, cross-fitted leave-one-trajectory-out; rank correlation with peak context 0.64 (Terminal-Bench) and 0.56 (SWE-bench Pro), log-error standard deviation 0.54 and 0.34.
load_bearing_assumption: That the hit rate is a function of the working-set ratio $W/C$ alone and that the session population closes the loop only through recorded tool gaps and call completion. Both are strained by the paper's own text. (1) The model 'uses the real-system hit-rate curve in Fig. 6b' (sec. 5.1), yet sec. 5.2 reports the opposite: 'This is cache hysteresis: similar demand for cached context produces different hit rates because the cached contents differ.' (hit rate 0.26-0.37 after collapse at $W = 1.6$-$1.7\,C$ against 0.81-0.93 in no-surge runs at the same working set). A one-dimensional model in $N$ with a static $h(W/C)$ has no state for cache contents, so the recovery boundary it predicts is the healthy branch's, and the paper falls back to measured collapsed-state departures (0.20-0.31 of $\lambda_{\mathrm{ref}}$) to size the recovery. (2) The workload is a replay: 'Each call becomes eligible after its predecessor completes and the recorded tool gap elapses.' (sec. 7.1). Sessions never abandon, retry, time out or shorten under slow service, so the only sustaining effect is the cache; the classic metastability sustaining effects the paper itself lists ('Retries, garbage collection and cold look-aside caches are known sustaining effects [31]', sec. 2) are absent by construction, and the trapped-state boundary measured here is the boundary for a client that waits forever. (3) For Basin specifically, that tool-idle context should be reserved at its predicted peak for the whole session: 'The prediction stays fixed until completion' (sec. 6.1), so a session that compacts or ends early still holds its reservation.
weakest_component: The hardware result and the full method are not the same system. (1) 'The hardware prototype uses arrival-time ordering and current-context admission (§6.6); the predictor-driven controller is evaluated in simulation from §7.3 on.' (sec. 7.2). The 1.20-1.70$\times$ Continuum and 2.35-3.59$\times$ HiCache numbers on real H200 1P3D come from a controller without the size-aware priority or the peak-context reservations; the 1.20-2.05$\times$ figures for the complete policy are simulated, on a simulator whose H200 goodput differs from the fifteen calibration runs 'by 8.8% on average and at most 32%', which 'overestimates ThunderAgent and Crossflow by 33% and 37%' out of calibration, and 'For the composition, it predicts 2.6 $\times$ the measured goodput.' (sec. 7.10); it also 'underestimates Basin's ITL-violating session share, at 0.5% against 13.6% measured.' (2) One model, one engine: 'All hardware experiments serve the hybrid MoE model Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on SGLang.' (sec. 9), a model whose 30 of 40 layers are linear attention with fixed-size recurrent state, so 'recurrent-state slots impose another capacity constraint' (sec. 2) that a full-attention model does not have. (3) The vulnerability classifier is $28/36$ correct: 'It also flags eight of the 19 decode-first deployments, giving 28 correct classifications (78%).' (sec. 5.1), so the headline 'flags all 17 cache-first cases' is recall with a 42% false-positive rate on decode-first deployments. (4) Baseline ports are the authors': the CONCUR hit-rate threshold is moved 'from 0.2 to 0.7 to place it within the observed range' (sec. 7.1) and ThunderAgent is a reimplementation in SGLang. (5) The predictor is weak and the paper shows it: rank correlation 0.56-0.64; 'Supplying exact peak contexts raises goodput by 1.27-1.35 $\times$ in the plotted scenarios' and true peaks perturbed by lognormal error with $\sigma = 1.0$ still beat the predictor by 1.15-1.19$\times$ (sec. 7.9), so most of the admission gain is left on the table and the ranking, not the magnitude, carries what is captured. (6) The profiled cliff, the paper's named instrument, is nearly inert in Basin: 'Scaling the profiled cliff by 0.5–2 $\times$ changes goodput by at most 1%, as the capacity term sets the bound.' (sec. 7.9).
regime: Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B in FP8, a hybrid linear-attention MoE (30 linear-attention layers of 40). Engine: SGLang PD disaggregation with NIXL transfers, page size 64; prefix radix cache on prefill with LRU eviction; HiCache host tier where stated. Hardware: H100 NVL 1P1D (prefill 1.09M-token prefix cache, decode 1.66M tokens KV, sec. 3.1; the surge and burst experiments) and one four-H200 node in 1P3D (the Basin comparisons); 2P6D only in simulation. Workloads: 216 replayed Terminal-Bench trajectories, 7,108 calls, median prompt 25.6K tokens, p90 77K, 98.2% of prompt tokens repeated from the preceding call, median output 160 tokens, median tool gap 0.42 s, median peak context 40K; 70 SWE-bench Pro sessions (median prompt 83K, median peak 107K, median tool gap 48 ms); Poisson arrivals, warm start with 42 active sessions; Alibaba Bailian traces shape arrivals in one sweep. Loads: base 3.3 sessions/min on H100 1P1D, a tenth to a twelfth of saturated prefill throughput; ten-minute surges of +33% (recovers within twenty minutes) and +100% (trapped: median TTFT about 60 s, hit rate 0.95 to 0.27, goodput 17 against 138 sessions/h in the following hour, 123 to 43 sessions/h over the run); surges of $\times 3$ to $\times 6$ for 20 minutes in the sweeps; base loads 0.5-0.66 of the profiled critical rate; trapping load 0.46-0.70 of steady-state overload across GPU and host-tier sweeps (sec. 4.2). Metric: goodput = completed sessions per hour with slowdown at most 4 and at least 95% of decode steps within a 50 ms ITL SLO; shed or rejected sessions count as failed. Runs 2 h (2.5 h with tool time $\times 3$). Horizon: tens of turns per session; sessions live minutes. Compute: dollar cost and total GPU-hours not reported (unknown, not in text). Venue: cs.DC preprint, 2026-11-02; NTU Singapore (Ustiugov group).
information_asymmetry: The serving gateway knows the per-session working set, each session's predicted peak context, the aggregate $W/C$, the queue states $Q_P$ and $Q_D$, the hit rate and the lent capacity, none of which the agent or the trainer ever sees; the agent and the trainer know, per session, the quantities the gateway has to predict: how many calls remain, how long the next tool will run, whether the session ends or compacts at the next turn, and, in RL, what the session is worth. (1) Gateway side. The signal that predicts the trap is the aggregate context of active sessions including tool-idle ones; the standard metrics do not carry it: 'Utilization, queue length and KV usage, commonly used for scaling and overload control [42, 92, 74, 67], all show ample headroom and give little warning of the failure.' (sec. 1) and 'KV usage can remain low while tool-idle sessions accumulate prefix demand, whereas a fixed cache-capacity budget can delay admission even while reuse remains high' (sec. 1). Basin computes $W = N\bar{c}$ from session tracking at the gateway, not from an engine counter; no agent or RL framework reads it. (2) Agent side, unused by the gateway. The gateway's $\hat{W}_i$ is a ridge regression on 'the task text and first-prompt length visible at that call' (sec. 6.1), rank correlation 0.56-0.64, while the agent harness holds the turn cap, the compaction threshold and the tool it is about to call; the paper's own oracle shows what that information is worth: exact peaks give 1.27-1.35$\times$ the predictor's goodput (sec. 7.9), and $K$ (calls per session) and $g$ (tool gap) enter eq. 1 as workload means the engine estimates but the harness sets. A harness that declared its remaining turns and its next tool duration at each call would turn the predictor into a lookup; nothing in the paper takes such a hint. (3) Trainer side, the lane's workload. In the paper $\lambda(t)$ is an exogenous Poisson stream and recovery needs 'a greater reduction in arrivals' (sec. 5.2); in asynchronous agentic RL the arrival stream is the rollout controller's own submission rate and the sessions are rollouts whose value the trainer knows (zero-advantage groups, stale samples). Basin's shedding drops 'the lowest-priority parked session' by arrival-plus-size (sec. 6.4), blind to value; a trainer could shed by advantage and set $\lambda$ below $D_{\mathrm{low}}$ on purpose. The engine, in turn, never learns which sessions are discardable. (4) Cache history vs demand. The engine's cached contents, not the working set, decide the hit rate after a collapse ('similar demand for cached context produces different hit rates because the cached contents differ', sec. 5.2); the model in $N$ alone cannot see this, and no exported metric names it. (5) Relative to the pipeline's L3 threads: eq. 2 is a second regime-sorting rule for PD topologies alongside CL-W43-07's temporal-overlap statistic (both say the payoff of a topology is a workload-by-resource ratio, here $f$, the fraction of sessions in service, set by tool time); Basin's activation at $B_0$ with release at $\alpha_R B_0$ plus cool-down is the backlog-threshold rule with hysteresis that CL-W43-08 asks whether a forecaster can beat, and the paper's forecaster is of per-session size, not of demand; and for the killed CL-W43-12 (residency binds before decode), this paper is a third serving-side confirmation in print (cache-first at 1P3D for every evaluated tool time, sec. 4.2), closing that door further rather than reopening it.
occupies: Published and not claimable: that a finite surge leaves a PD-disaggregated agent-serving engine degraded at a previously sustained base load (SGLang, H100 1P1D, +100% for ten minutes: goodput 138 to 17 sessions/h in the following hour) and that removing the residual burst sessions restores service within two minutes; the name population-cache feedback for the loop in which cache misses lengthen sessions and sessions enlarge the working set; the fluid model (eqs. 1-4) with its stable and unstable equilibria, the memory criterion $C \lesssim D_{\mathrm{KV}}/(2f)$ for cache-first versus decode-first deployments, the cache cliff near $W \approx 1.9\,C$, cache hysteresis after collapse, and the post-surge arrival intervention showing that changing only subsequent arrivals reverses recovery; the Basin controller (fixed arrival-plus-predicted-size priority on all queues, Denning working-set admission on predicted peak contexts with page-fault-frequency budget adaptation, idle decode memory lent as a prefix-cache tier under reclamation rules, shedding above the profiled peak departure rate) and its numbers (real H200 1P3D 1.20-1.70$\times$ Continuum, 2.35-3.59$\times$ HiCache; simulated 1.20-2.05$\times$ the strongest baseline). Left open by the paper's own text: colocated engines ('the corresponding model bounds would reflect that shared resource pool', sec. 9), dependent parent-child sessions, capacity changes between profiles, any model beyond one hybrid MoE on SGLang, a predictor that uses harness-side information, and the RL-rollout case where arrivals are chosen rather than suffered.

neighbors.title: Continuum: Efficient and Robust Multi-Turn LLM Agent Scheduling with KV Cache Time-to-Live
neighbors.trick: Pin a tool-calling request's KV in GPU memory for a time-to-live set from the reload cost and the queueing delay eviction would cause, and serve programs first-come-first-served; the paper's strongest baseline, whose 'age order is the case of Basin's fixed priority in which all working-set estimates are equal' (sec. 8), and whose TTL pinning, the paper finds, stays within 1% of LRU.

neighbors.title: ThunderAgent: A Simple, Fast and Program-Aware Agentic Inference System
neighbors.trick: Abstract an agent workflow as an LLM Program and schedule its KV cache, sandbox state and tool assets end to end with a program-aware scheduler that admits sessions against the larger cache tier; the paper's admission baseline, which 'ties its bound to the larger prefill cache tier' and so holds new sessions 26-39 minutes at the gateway while preserving reuse (sec. 7.2, 7.5).

neighbors.title: CONCUR: High-Throughput Agentic Batch Inference of LLM via Congestion-Based Concurrency Control
neighbors.trick: Treat the KV cache as a congested shared link and adjust the number of active agents from runtime cache signals (KV usage, hit rate) to stop middle-phase thrashing in offline agent batches; the paper's concurrency-control baseline, whose signals miss tool-idle demand: 'At equal decode occupancy, different numbers of tool-idle sessions impose different cache demand, and the hit-rate trigger responds only after reuse deteriorates.' (sec. 7.5).

neighbors.title: Crossflow: Prefill-Decode Elasticity for Agentic LLM Serving
neighbors.trick: Let each decode node publish a short revocable lease that lets it run some prefill locally, so the prefill-decode boundary flexes with the uncached-input-to-output ratio without reassigning nodes; the paper's capacity baseline, which borrows decode compute where Basin borrows only decode memory, and which stays trapped in all four hardware scenarios because prefill on decode nodes competes with generation (sec. 7.2, 7.5).

neighbors.title: Service-Induced Congestion in Memory-Constrained LLM Serving
neighbors.trick: Model continuous batching with growing per-request KV as a discrete-time dynamical system and prove that under saturated input the eviction-free equilibrium is unstable and the system converges to a limit cycle of evictions costing up to 50% throughput; the paper cites it as 'instability from KV growth' (sec. 8) and differs by making the state the session population across tool calls and the instability a trigger-dependent bistability rather than a cycle.

theme_fit.why: prefix-cache reuse under agentic load, a PD-topology regime criterion (cache-first vs decode-first by tool time), session admission and shedding, and the true cost of tool-idle context are the lane sentence verbatim; it also bears on CL-W43-07 (second regime rule for PD payoff), CL-W43-08 (a threshold-with-hysteresis controller in print) and the killed CL-W43-12 (third confirmation that residency binds before decode in 1P3D)

the demand is context growth across turns ($\bar{c}$, peak context), which compaction would shrink, but the paper never compacts; the serving lever is counted under L3's 'compaction as a serving and cost lever'
same words (rollout, arrivals, shedding) different problem; the RL analogue, where the trainer controls $\lambda(t)$ and knows which sessions are worth finishing, is not in the paper

limitations_as_complaints: My model and every hardware number are for PD-disaggregated SGLang serving one hybrid MoE, and the complete controller exists only in a simulator that misses some baselines by 2.6x: 'All hardware experiments serve the hybrid MoE model Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on SGLang.' (sec. 9); 'In colocated deployments, prefill and decode share compute and memory; the corresponding model bounds would reflect that shared resource pool.' (sec. 9); 'The hardware prototype uses arrival-time ordering and current-context admission (§6.6); the predictor-driven controller is evaluated in simulation from §7.3 on.' (sec. 7.2); 'For the composition, it predicts 2.6 $\times$ the measured goodput.' (sec. 7.10). Whether colocated engines, verl/SGLang rollout workers in RL, or a full-attention model show the same trap is not shown.

My admission reserves each session's peak context from a text regression with rank correlation 0.56-0.64, and my own oracle says I leave a quarter to a third of the goodput on the table: 'The predictor uses the task text and first-prompt length visible at that call (§6.5).' (sec. 6.1); 'Supplying exact peak contexts raises goodput by 1.27–1.35 $\times$ in the plotted scenarios and 1.10–1.51 $\times$ across triggers, showing further benefit from improved predictions.' (sec. 7.9). The harness that runs the agent knows its turn cap, its compaction rule and its next tool, and I never ask it.

I assume independent sessions and fixed capacity between profiles, which rules out multi-agent workflows and autoscaling: 'The evaluated trajectories consist of independent sessions. Parent–child workflows couple their lifetimes: a parent can retain context while its child waits for service.' and 'These workflows therefore call for dependency-aware ordering, admission and prefix accounting.' (sec. 9); 'Basin assumes fixed capacity between profiles. Adding [42], switching or losing an instance changes the cliff, with new cache capacity becoming useful only as it warms.' (sec. 9).
